deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. Gauss sets up a parabolic comet orbit from three observations. The page shows the general preparatory reductions, then a discussion of which great circle through the middle place to use; the next page continues with the key equation.

The dates are April 7.55, 14.55 and 21.60 (Sun longitude about 18 to 32 degrees). The bundle is 1813, so this is very probably the first comet of 1813 (Pons, April 1813); that identification is unsure.

DATA.
- Times: t, t', t''.
- Geocentric ecliptic longitudes a, a', a'' and latitudes b, b', b''.
- Sun longitudes T, T', T''.
- log Earth–Sun distances log R, log R', log R''. The label 'Abstaende von der Erde' means the Sun's distances from the Earth.

STEP 1: elongation and least distance (ours: the geometry).
- With l the unit vector to the comet and the Sun at R(cos T, sin T, 0), cos psi = cos b cos(a - T). Here psi is the elongation.
- Heliocentric r^2 = rho^2 - 2 rho R cos psi + R^2 = A^2 + (rho - R cos psi)^2, with A = R sin psi. This is the form used for rr and r''r'' on the next page.
- Numbers: log cos b = 9.94168, log cos(a - T) = 9.45379n, so log cos psi = 9.39547n. Then log sin psi = 9.98615 and log A = 9.98706.
- Likewise log cos psi'' = 9.84086n, log sin psi'' = 9.85778, log A'' = 9.86038.

STEP 2: chord of the Sun's geocentric positions between the 1st and 3rd dates (ours: interpretation).
- f e_F = R'' e_T'' - R e_T, i.e. R'' cos(T'' - T) - R = f cos(F - T) and R'' sin(T'' - T) = f sin(F - T).
- Numbers: log[R'' cos(T'' - T)] = 9.99001. Subtracting R by a Gaussian (subtraction) logarithm gives 8.39501n. log[R'' sin] = 9.37795.
- So F - T = 95°56'16'' (second quadrant), F = 113°43'57''.
- log f = 9.37795 - log sin(F - T) = 9.37795 - 9.99766 = 9.38029.

STEP 3: great circle C through the 1st and 3rd geocentric places, with node Om and inclination i.
- Condition: tan b = tan i sin(a - Om).
- Expanding tan b'' = tan i sin((a'' - a) + (a - Om)) gives [tan b'' - tan b cos(a'' - a)]/sin(a'' - a) = tan i cos(a - Om).
- Numerator: 0.17429 - 0.53744 = -0.36315, log 9.56010n. log sin(a'' - a) = 9.39786n, so log[tan i cos(a - Om)] = 0.16224.
- Hence log tan(a - Om) = 9.74435 - 0.16224 = 9.58211, a - Om = 20°54'32'', Om = 250°22'6''.
- log tan i = 0.19183 (i about 57°15'), log sin i = 9.92487, log cos i = 9.73304.
- Derived angles: a' - Om = 16°5'16''; a'' - Om = 6°26'2''; F - Om = 223°21'51''.

STEP 4: arguments of l and l'' within C, measured from the node.
- tan K = tan(a - Om)/cos i, giving K = 35°14'19''.
- tan K'' = tan(a'' - Om)/cos i, giving K'' = 11°46'42''.

STEP 5: resolve the vector f e_F into components relative to C (ours: interpretation).
- Along the node line: f cos(F - Om). In-plane perpendicular: f cos i sin(F - Om). Normal to C: f sin i sin(F - Om).
- The in-plane part is written in polar form: g sin G = f cos i sin(F - Om) and g cos G = f cos(F - Om). The arithmetic uses cos(F - Om), log 9.86154n.
- Numbers: 8.95005n and 9.24183n give G = 207°3'23'' (third quadrant) and log g = 9.29217.
- On the next page the comet chord becomes |rho'' e_K'' - rho e_K - g e_G|^2 + (f sin i sin(F - Om))^2, which is exactly the 'Chorde^2' expression there.

STEP 6: the point Q.
- Correct geometry (ours): the great circle through the middle place (a', b') perpendicular to C passes through the pole n = (0, -sin i, cos i) of C, in the frame with x toward Om.
- Its ecliptic intersection q ∝ cos i p' - sin b' n gives tan(Q - Om) = tan(a' - Om) + tan i tan b'/cos(a' - Om) = tan(a' - Om)[1 + tan i tan b'/sin(a' - Om)]. This is the final, uncancelled formula on the page.
- The main column, however, computes 1 + sin(a' - Om) cot i cot b' (logs 9.44265 + 9.80817 + 0.37486 = 9.62568, giving 0.15301). That is the crossed-out inverted variant.
- It yields Q - Om = 22°18'15'' and Q = 272°40'21'', with T' - Q = 111°58'24'', a - Q = -1°23'43'', etc.
- The partly legible margin column redoes this with the correct formula: log tan(Q - Om) ≈ 9.9873, Q - Om ≈ 44°9'45'', Q ≈ 294°31'51''. The differences follow: T' - Q ≈ 90°7', a - Q ≈ -23°15', a' - Q ≈ -28°4', a'' - Q ≈ -37°44', T - Q ≈ 83°16', T'' - Q ≈ 96°60'.

STEP 7: text.
- The 1-3 data are over-determined. Keep only the condition that the middle place lies on one chosen great circle through it, meeting the ecliptic at longitude P.
- P = Sun's place is Olbers' convenient choice, but it is sometimes not sharp enough.
- P = Om represents only the curvature of the apparent path. P = Q represents only the change of speed, and generally gives the sharpest result.
- The page then announces the rigorous equation using Theoria Motus' n, n', n'' and k; it appears on p. 21.
errors: The node/Q computation: the worked value Q - Om = 22°18'15'' comes from tan(Q - Om) = tan(a' - Om)(1 + sin(a' - Om) cot i cot b'), the struck-out inverted form. The geometrically correct form, kept on the page, gives Q - Om ≈ 44°9'45''. Gauss evidently noticed this and recomputed in the margin (44.9.., 294.3.., 90.., -23.1.., etc.). However, the next page still uses the first Q (e.g. log sin(T' - Q) = 9.96725 = log sin 111°58'24''). This is harmless in principle, since P is arbitrary, but it is not the intended optimal P.
The arithmetic for g, G uses f cos(F - Om) = g cos G. If the page really reads 'f sin(F - Om) = g cos G', that formula is a slip; the computation is right.
The value 9.99766 labelled 'cos(F - T)' is actually log sin(F - T) = log sin 95°56'16''. The use is correct, the label is wrong (slip or transcription).
There are minor last-digit discrepancies only: e.g. log sin i computes to 9.92489 vs 9.92487, and 0.15302 vs 0.15301, both negligible. All other logs and angles check to 5 places / 1''.

results.what: Reduction of three geocentric observations: elongation psi, least distance A = R sin psi, so that r^2 = A^2 + (rho - R cos psi)^2
results.modern_name: standard preliminary reduction in Olbers'/Gauss' parabolic orbit determination

results.what: Great circle through the 1st and 3rd geocentric places (node Om, inclination i), with in-circle arguments K, K'' and the decomposition of the Earth chord (f, F) into in-plane (g, G) and normal f sin i sin(F - Om) components
results.modern_name: spherical-trigonometric setup for the chord (Euler/Lambert) equation

results.what: Replacing Olbers' great circle through the Sun by an arbitrary great circle through the middle place, with the optimal choice perpendicular to the 1-3 circle (P = Q), and the remark that P = Om constrains only curvature and P = Q only speed
results.modern_name: generalised Olbers method / choice of auxiliary great circle to avoid the Olbers failure case
results.usually_credited_to: discussed by Gauss and Encke (19th c.); the Olbers failure case is well known

deep.surprise_reason: This is competent, routine orbit-computation work in Gauss's established style; the arithmetic is correct apart from one corrected formula. The only mildly notable point is the explicit general-P version of Olbers' method, with the perpendicular circle recommended as sharpest. Such modifications are known in the Gauss/Encke literature, so this is at most a minor unpublished detail.

transcription_corrections: The second g, G relation as used numerically is f cos(F-Ω) = g cos G.
The struck-out first expression is tang(α'-Ω)(1 + sin(α'-Ω)/(tg i tg b')), the one actually used in the column arithmetic.

The right margin numbers next to the Q column are a recomputation with the correct formula: approximately 9.9873, Q-Ω = 44°9'45'', Q = 294°31'51'', Θ'-Q = 90°7', α-Q = -23°15', α'-Q = -28°4', α''-Q = -37°44', Θ-Q = 83°16', Θ''-Q = 96°60'.
